data.cultural_impact: In Islamic culture, the name Zakoor is a symbol ofbravery, strength, and protection. A man with the name Zakoor is often seen as a reliable and trusted friend and ally. In Arabic folklore, there is a tale of a brave warrior named Zakoor, who protected his people from enemies. This name is commonly used in the Arab world and among the Muslim diaspora.
data.spiritual_significance: From a spiritual perspective, the name Zakoor represents the idea of God as a protector and shield. In the Quran, Allah is often referred to as 'Al-Muhaimin' or the Protector, and 'Ar-Raqaab' or the Watcher. The name Zakoor is a reminder of the divine protection that Allah provides to his believers. It encourages the bearer to seek refuge in Allah and trust in his protection. Furthermore, the name Zakoor challenges the bearer to be a protector of others, reflecting the Hadith that 'Whosoever relieves a believer of a calamity, Allah will save him from a calamity.' (Sahih Muslim). This name can serve as a constant reminder of the importance of kindness, compassion, and protection towards others.

historical_references.reference: Ibn Khaldun describes Zakoor as a North African Berber city which was the capital of the Hafsid dynasty in the 14th century.
historical_references.context: Ibn Khaldun's 'Muqaddimah' is a historical and sociological work where he describes various cities and dynasties of the Islamic world, including Zakoor, the capital of the Hafsid Berber kingdom in North Africa.

historical_references.reference: Al-Idrisi mentions Zakoor as a city located in the Maghreb region, which was an important stopover on the trans-Saharan trade routes in the 12th century.
historical_references.context: Al-Idrisi was a 12th-century Muslim geographer and cartographer. He wrote a comprehensive geographical work, 'Nuzhat al-Mushtaq fi Ikhtiraq al-Afqaq', which describes various regions of the Islamic world, including Zakoor, a city in the Maghreb that was an important stopover on the trans-Saharan trade routes.
